submission.natural_language_explanation: The negative pole fires on a token that is part of the proper name of a specific named entity - a country, city, organisation, sports team, newspaper, brand or person - both when the name is a single token (' Giants' 1.18, ' Tigers' 1.14, ' Economist' 0.76, ' Maurit'+'ania' 0.66/0.35, ' Nigeria' 0.28) and for every piece of a multi-token name (' United'+' States' 0.56/0.27, ' District'+' of'+' Columbia'), and lower-case spellings fire just as hard (' united states' 0.87/0.35). Ordinary common nouns and function words in exactly the same slots stay near the floor (' team' 0.08, ' squad' 0.09, ' magazine' 0.10, ' market' 0.16, ' local court' 0.06), so the pole is not a capitalisation, token-rarity or surprisal detector (correlation with the current token's surprisal is -0.01 over 46k scanned tokens); its only other lifts are a clause-final period (about 0.10-0.25, straddling the 0.25x-scale line) and a named era written as an ordinal plus 'century' (' In the 11th century' 0.59, ' In the 19th century' 1.11), which I read as the same named-entity class rather than a second job.

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The harbour authority had spent nearly a decade arguing about how to keep the low-lying docks dry. Every winter the water crept a little higher, and every spring the engineers promised that the next round of upgrades would finally settle the question. The plans sat in committee for months, redrawn and re-costed, while the cranes kept working through the rain.

Most of the cargo that arrives by sea is packed into steel boxes, and the rhythm of the whole district depends on those boxes moving steadily from ship to rail to road. When a delay lasts more than a day, the trucks begin queueing along the approach roads, the warehouses fill beyond capacity, and the smaller operators start losing contracts to rivals with more space. The larger logistics firms tolerate the congestion because they can absorb the cost, but the family-run businesses cannot, and their complaints dominate every public meeting.

A second problem is the labour force. Fewer young people want to work nights on the quays, and the training programmes that once produced a steady stream of crane operators have shrunk. Managers say the shortage is manageable for now, but they worry about the decade ahead, when a large share of the current staff will retire. Automation is offered as the answer, although the unions point out that the newest terminals, which run almost without people, employ a fraction of the workers the old ones did.

Then there is the question of who pays. The national government funds the sea defences, the regional authority maintains the roads, and the port itself is expected to cover the internal infrastructure. Each body has its own budget cycle, its own priorities, and its own lawyers. Negotiations that ought to take a few weeks stretch into years, and the result is a patchwork of repairs rather than a single coherent plan.

Insurance is another complication. The companies that cover the warehouses have adjusted their premiums twice in recent years, and they now demand detailed surveys before renewing a policy. Smaller tenants say the paperwork alone takes weeks, and a few have moved inland rather than accept the new terms.

Visitors often remark on the strange mixture of scale and intimacy in a place like Rotterdam, where a container terminal the size of a small town sits a short walk from terraced houses, corner shops and a school. Residents have learned to live with the noise and the lights, and many say they would not trade the view of the water for anything quieter.

Officials now admit that the original timetable was optimistic. The next phase of work will begin once the funding is agreed, which they hope will be soon.
adversarial_test_results.detail: A single city name, present as the lone proper-name token ' Rotterdam' deep inside a long, different-genre passage with no other named entities, testing whether the pole still fires on the name when it is far from the start of the context.
